subject: biology

items.q: What is meant by food security?
items.correct: Having enough food to feed a population.
items.misconception: Growing a country's food within its borders.
items.why: The everyday word 'security' suggests self-defence and independence, and students hear about countries 'relying on imports' in the news, so they assume the measure is where the food is grown rather than whether there is enough of it. Food security is having enough food to feed a population. Where the food is produced is not part of the definition; changing diets in developed countries means scarce food resources are transported around the world, and this is listed as a factor affecting food security, not as the definition of it.
items.random_wrong: Storing enough food to survive any famine.

items.q: A new insect pest spreads into a country and destroys much of its wheat crop. Which biological factor affecting food security does this describe?
items.correct: New pests and pathogens that affect farming.
items.misconception: An increasing birth rate in some countries.
items.why: The everyday word 'security' suggests self-defence and independence, and students hear about countries 'relying on imports' in the news, so they assume the measure is where the food is grown rather than whether there is enough of it. Food security is having enough food to feed a population. Where the food is produced is not part of the definition; changing diets in developed countries means scarce food resources are transported around the world, and this is listed as a factor affecting food security, not as the definition of it.
items.random_wrong: Environmental change such as rains failing.

items.q: A farmer rears animals for meat indoors. Which change would improve the efficiency of food production?
items.correct: Limit movement and control the temperature.
items.misconception: Give them more space in which to move around.
items.why: Students know that exercise is healthy and that being hot is uncomfortable, so they assume free movement and cool conditions must be the efficient option; they also forget that a mammal in cold surroundings transfers more energy to the environment while keeping its body temperature constant. The efficiency of food production can be improved by restricting energy transfer from food animals to the environment. This can be done by limiting their movement and by controlling the temperature of their surroundings, so less of the energy in their food is transferred to the environment and more is available for growth.
items.random_wrong: Keep them in cool, well ventilated buildings.

items.q: Why are some food animals fed high protein foods?
items.correct: To increase their rate of growth.
items.misconception: To give them energy for movement.
items.why: Students meet protein in the diet alongside carbohydrate and lipid and remember that food releases energy, so they treat every extra nutrient as an energy supply rather than as raw material for new tissue. Some animals are fed high protein foods to increase growth. The protein is used for growth, which raises the efficiency of food production; energy transfer to the environment is restricted separately by limiting movement and controlling the temperature of the surroundings.

items.q: Fish stocks in one area of ocean are declining. Which action would help to conserve the stocks at a sustainable level?
items.correct: Use fishing quotas and control the net size.
items.misconception: Remove quotas and keep the net size the same.
items.why: Students know that fish produce huge numbers of eggs and that the oceans are vast, so they assume the population can replace itself at any level of fishing. Fish stocks in the oceans are declining. It is important to maintain fish stocks at a level where breeding continues, or certain species may disappear altogether in some areas, so limits on fishing are needed.
items.random_wrong: Use small mesh nets to catch the young fish.

items.q: Mycoprotein is a protein-rich food suitable for vegetarians. How is it produced?
items.correct: Fusarium is grown on glucose syrup, in aerobic conditions.
items.misconception: Bacteria are grown on glucose syrup, in aerobic conditions.
items.why: Students meet bacteria far more often than fungi in biotechnology examples, and they associate industrial vats of microorganisms with anaerobic fermentation such as brewing. The fungus Fusarium is useful for producing mycoprotein, a protein-rich food suitable for vegetarians. The fungus is grown on glucose syrup, in aerobic conditions, and the biomass is harvested and purified.
items.random_wrong: Fusarium is grown on glucose syrup, in anaerobic conditions.

items.q: Golden rice is a genetically modified crop. How can GM crops help to meet the demands of the growing human population?
items.correct: By providing more food or improved nutrition.
items.misconception: By providing medicines inside the food eaten.
items.why: Students know that some microorganisms live in the human gut and hear about 'good bacteria' in foods, so they assume the modified bacterium is delivered into the body rather than used as a factory outside it. A genetically modified bacterium produces human insulin. When harvested and purified this is used to treat people with diabetes; it is the insulin, not the bacterium, that is given to the patient.
items.random_wrong: By providing more food, not improved nutrition.

items.q: Which kinds of factor are threatening food security?
items.correct: Biological factors threatening food security include the increasing birth rate, changing diets in developed countries, new pests and pathogens, environmental changes such as failed rains, the cost of agricultural inputs, and conflicts affecting the availability of water or food.
items.misconception: Food security is only threatened by environmental changes such as rains failing, because famine is what causes people to go short of food.
items.why: Images of drought and famine dominate media coverage of food shortages, so students treat environmental change as the single cause and overlook the other factors listed in the specification. Environmental changes that affect food production, such as widespread famine occurring in some countries if rains fail, are only one of the biological factors listed. The increasing birth rate, changing diets in developed countries, new pests and pathogens that affect farming, the cost of agricultural inputs, and conflicts that affect the availability of water or food all threaten food security as well.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is food security the same thing as sustainable food production?
items.correct: Food security is having enough food to feed a population; separately, sustainable methods must be found to feed all people on Earth.
items.misconception: Food security means producing food in a way that does not damage the environment, so a country with environmentally friendly farming automatically has food security.
items.why: The two ideas appear in the same specification point and are often taught in the same lesson, so students merge them into a single definition. Food security is having enough food to feed a population. Sustainability is a separate requirement: sustainable methods must be found to feed all people on Earth, so that food production can continue in the future.

items.q: How does controlling net size help to conserve fish stocks?
items.correct: Control of net size, along with fishing quotas, conserves fish stocks at a sustainable level; a larger mesh size allows young fish to escape so that breeding continues.
items.misconception: Using nets with a smaller mesh size conserves fish stocks, because smaller nets catch fewer fish.
items.why: Students read 'small net' as 'small catch' and picture the overall size of the net rather than the size of the holes in the mesh. Control of net size and the introduction of fishing quotas play important roles in conservation of fish stocks at a sustainable level. A larger mesh size lets young fish pass through the net so they survive to breed, maintaining stocks at a level where breeding continues.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What can genetically modified crops provide?
items.correct: GM crops could provide more food or food with an improved nutritional value such as golden rice.
items.misconception: Genetically modified crops can only increase the amount of food produced; they cannot change how nutritious the food is.
items.why: GM crops are usually introduced through examples of higher yield and pest resistance, so students remember quantity and never meet an example where the nutritional value of the food itself is changed. GM crops could provide more food or food with an improved nutritional value, such as golden rice, so genetic modification can change the quality of the food as well as the quantity produced.
